claims.text: A predictive model that explicitly incorporates alloy-induced mass and strain fluctuations will identify low-lattice-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than models that neglect these factors.
Debye temperature, Grüneisen parameter, and dominant phonon wavelength can serve as model descriptors related to phonon-mediated thermal transport.
GeTe-based and PbSe-based multicomponent chalcogenide solid solutions are high-entropy compounds.
The cited GeTe-based and PbSe-based high-entropy compounds are relevant to mid- and high-temperature applications.
The cited compounds are relevant specifically to thermal-insulation applications.
First-principles calculations can be used to obtain Debye temperature, thermal conductivity, Grüneisen parameter, and dominant phonon wavelength for these alloy systems.
First-principles-derived phonon descriptors can be used to estimate phonon-scattering efficiency and thereby predict thermal conductivity.
Alloy-induced mass and strain fluctuations are measurably reflected in shifts in Debye temperature, Grüneisen parameter, and dominant phonon wavelength.
Increased mass and strain variations enhance phonon scattering.
Strengthening phonon scattering reduces lattice thermal conductivity.
Including mass- and strain-related descriptors will produce closer agreement between predicted and experimentally observed thermal conductivity.
The proposed approach will reduce median absolute thermal-conductivity prediction error by approximately 20% relative to traditional models.
Existing baseline models rely primarily on nominal composition and omit detailed phonon-scattering effects associated with mass and strain redistribution.
The model will be most effective for high-entropy alloys having compositional and structural disorder similar to the GeTe-based and PbSe-based reference systems.
The model's applicability may be limited in systems with substantially different bonding characteristics or phase separation.
The exact error reduction and transferability beyond alloys similar to the reference systems are uncertain.
An improvement of less than approximately 20% over the baseline would falsify the stated quantitative prediction.
A substantial disagreement between the predicted and experimental ranking of low-thermal-conductivity alloys would falsify the hypothesis.
